To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sexual differences which “matter” in early modern English culture do not exactly coincide with those which matter today, that the beard was a central means of making masculinity “matter” during the period in question, that this was true both on and off stage, and that the beard was not simply a means of materializing the difference between men and women, but was also a means of making a difference between men and boys.
facial hair was a crucial means of constructing masculinity in early modern English society, and that this was not a stable, fixed, or essentialist process.

the beard mattered in early modern England because it was an important marker of masculinity and that this was the case not only because it was an essential part of a man's body but because it was also a prosthetic part of his costume and makeup.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which the beard helped to make men in early modern England.
the ways in which Renaissance culture imagined and performed sexual differences between men, women, boys, and men
the ways in which the body, and in particular the body of the Renaissance actor, was constructed and represented as a site of sexual and gender difference.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Renaissance masculinity was constructed by means of a beard that was itself constructed.
the beard is a material means of making the man, but the man is a material means for making the beard.
the beard is a material signifier of the masculine, and that it was the beard that made the man in early modern England.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Renaissance beards matter.
we have tried to show the importance of the beard in early modern England.
the Renaissance Beard is the first book that examines Renaissance masculinity through a study of facial hair.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we need to be very careful when we use the term “gender” to refer to early modern sexual differences, since the term is so closely associated with the “modern” notion of gender as something that is socially constructed. In
the Renaissance beard was not simply a signifier of masculinity, but a means of constructing masculinity in the first place.
we need to be more attentive to the materiality of the body, and to the ways in which it was constructed in early modern England.
